newsitem.title: CHINA: China share issues cause market indigestion.
newsitem.headline: China share issues cause market indigestion.

text.p: Prices on China's two stock exchanges have fallen around 15 percent in the week since Hong Kong's return to China, choked by new offers designed to cool speculation before the handover, analysts said on Tuesday.

By midday on Tuesday, Shanghai's domestic A share index had plunged 14.20 percent to 1,121.23 points from the close on June 27, the last trading day before Hong Kong's 156 years as a British colony came to an end on July 1.
The foreign currency B share index had shed 12.96 percent, while in Shenzhen, the A share index had lost 18.84 percent and the B share index 16.21 percent.

"The central government purposefully allowed a large number of companies with hundreds of millions of shares to debut each day in the leadup to the handover to curb speculation," said an analyst with a major Chinese brokerage.
"The markets are suffering from indigestion with current liquidity unable to quickly absorb the new shares," he said.
"The new share bombardment has sent a chilly message to the markets that the central government still regards the current level of the share indices as too high," said a second analyst.
"This has fuelled widespread market rumours that new official crackdown measures are taking shape," she said.

The markets have been awash with rumours this week that Beijing is planning to allow the listing of some of the massive quantities of China's non-tradable institutional and state shares, brokers said.
Officials have declined to comment.
The about face on the markets is in stark contrast to the feverish rally before Hong Kong's handover.
On June 26 alone, 10 firms debuted, flooding the market with a combined 480 million shares on a market capitalisation of around 6.5 billion yuan ($783 million).
On June 27, another six firms with a total of 208 million shares debuted on China's bourses.
Disappointment that Hong Kong's media-hyped handover has not inspired the market as hoped has compounded official measures introduced over the past couple of months to cool speculation.
In May and June, Beijing banned state banks, state enterprises and listed firms from trading on the stock markets.
It also suspended four major securities brokerages from trading on their own accounts because of irregularities.
"Money supply to the stock markets has effectively been cut with some major institutions unable to trade, adding to the weight of the new shares," an A share trader said.

"Investors are beginning to feel that no matter what shares they buy, they cannot sell them without a loss in the short term. This will prevent any sizeable buying over the coming few weeks," said a stock investment researcher.
Most analysts agreed the markets would see further losses, but said they expected the indices to find firm support after falling another five to 10 percent in the next few days.
Analysts said investors felt that with the Hong Kong handover a done deal, there were no short-term stimuli on the horizon.
Listed firms' 1997 interim results, due to be released by August 31, were not expected to provide any good news, analysts said, because many companies had done poorly in the past two years.

But there were two major mid-term positive factors, they said: China's macro-economic outlook for 1997 was healthy, and the Chinese Communist Party was due to convene its four-yearly national congress in October, which could offer the markets fresh speculative topics.
